e-470.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
e-470.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\textrm{d}u = \arcsin(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $9x^2 = (3x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \,\textrm d u=\textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{4\sqrt{1-9{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(3x)^{2}}}\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{12}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡3x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

e-471.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
e-471.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \dfrac{3}{2 + 50x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{3}{2(1 + 25x^2)} = \dfrac 3 2 \int \dfrac{1}{1+25x^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+u^2}\textrm{d}u =\arctan u +C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $25x^2 = (5x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 5\,\textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{2+50{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+25{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+(5x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡5x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

e-5014.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant
e-5014.worked_solution:
This resembles the basic integral for $\textrm{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

Let $u = 5x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
5\,\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5\,\text{d}x}{|5x|\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(5x)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

e-472.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Trigonometric Functions
e-472.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+{x}^{2}/2)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this integral now resembles the basic integral for the inverse tangent,

$$
\int\dfrac{1}{1+u^2}\,\textrm d u = \arctan{u} + C.
$$

We make the substitution $u=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt 2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt 2 \,\textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡u|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡1-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:   

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{3\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{8}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/4)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}.$ 

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

 

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{3\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{4}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (2\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

∫834−x2dx=83∫14⋅(1−x2/4)dx=83⋅12∫11−x2/4dx=43∫11−(x/2)2dx

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

∫11−u2du=arcsin⁡(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x2)2.

So, let's substitute u=x2. Differentiating, we get dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫834−x2dx=43∫11−(x/2)2dx=43∫11−u2⋅(2du)=83∫du1−u2=83arcsin⁡u+C=83arcsin⁡(x2)+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:   

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{3\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{8}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/4)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}.$ 

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

 

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{3\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{4}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (2\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substitute u=√3 x, so dx=du/√3. The integral becomes (3/√3)∫du/√(1-u²)=√3 arcsin(√3 x)+C.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $3{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{1-3{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ∫31−3x2dx.

a
33arcsin⁡(3x)+C
b
3arcsin⁡(3x)+C
c
3arcsin⁡(x)+C
d
3arcsin⁡(3x)+C

Submit

EXPLANATION

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine, ∫11−u2du=arcsin⁡(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have 3x2=(3x)2.

So, let's substitute u=3x. Differentiating, we get dudx=3⟹dx=13du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫31−3x2dx=3∫11−(3x)2dx=3∫11−u2⋅(13du)=33∫11−u2du=333arcsin⁡u+C=3arcsin⁡(3x)+C

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d. With u=√3 x, dx=du/√3, giving coefficient 3/√3=√3. Differentiating √3 arcsin(√3 x) yields 3/√(1−3x²), the original integrand.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $3{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{1-3{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Calculate ∫41−2x2dx.

a
2arcsin⁡(2x)+C
b
22arcsin⁡(2x)+C
c
2arcsin⁡(x)+C
d
2arcsin⁡(2x)+C
e
22arcsin⁡(2x)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine, ∫11−u2du=arcsin⁡(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have 2x2=(2x)2.

So, let's substitute u=2x. Differentiating, we get dudx=2⟹dx=12du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫41−2x2dx=4∫11−(2x)2dx=4∫11−u2⋅(12du)=42∫11−u2du=422arcsin⁡u+C=22arcsin⁡(2x)+C

$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $2{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}.$

$$

$$

decision.explanation: Let u=4x, so dx=du/4. Then the integral is (2/4)∫du/√(1−u²)=arcsin(4x)/2+C.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $16{x}^{2}=(4x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-16{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(4x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(4x)}{2}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $16{x}^{2}=(4x)^{2}.$

$$

$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x/5. Then dx=5 du and √(25−x²)=5√(1−u²), so the integral becomes 2∫du/√(1−u²)=2 arcsin(x/5)+C.

after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{25\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/25)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/25}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$ 

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get  

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (5\,\text{d}u) \\  & =2\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{5})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ∫225−x2dx.

a
2arcsin⁡(x5)+C
b
225arcsin⁡(x5)+C
c

d
2arcsin⁡(5x)+C

arcsin⁡(x5)+C

EXPLANATION

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

∫225−x2dx=2∫125⋅(1−x2/25)dx=25∫11−x2/25dx=25∫11−(x/5)2dx

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

∫11−u2du=arcsin⁡(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x5)2.

So, let's substitute u=x5. Differentiating, we get

dudx=15⟹dx=5du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫225−x2dx=25∫11−(x/5)2dx=25∫11−u2⋅(5du)=2∫du1−u2=2arcsin⁡u+C=2arcsin⁡(x5)+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{25\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/25)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/25}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$ 

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get  

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (5\,\text{d}u) \\  & =2\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{5})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{9}{81\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/81)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/81}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

 The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{9})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{9}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{9}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=9\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (9\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{9})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substitute u=4x, so dx=du/4. The integral becomes (1/4)∫du/(1+u²)=arctan(4x)/4+C.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $16{x}^{2}=(4x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(4x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4x)}{4}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $16{x}^{2}=(4x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(4x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4x)}{4}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{4\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/4)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}.$ 

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (2\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{4\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/4)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}.$ 

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (2\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{25+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{25\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/25)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/25}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/5)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{25+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/5)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (5\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{5})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Calculate ∫816+x2dx.

a
12arctan⁡(x4)+C
b
2arctan⁡(x4)+C
c
2arctan⁡(4x)+C
d
14arctan⁡(x4)+C
e
arctan⁡(x4)+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Let u=x/4, so dx=4 du and 16+x²=16(1+u²). The integral becomes 2∫du/(1+u²)=2 arctan(x/4)+C.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{16+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8}{16\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/16)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/16}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{16+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =2\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =2\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let's rewrite our integral as follows: ∫816+x2dx=∫816⋅(1+x2/16)dx=12∫11+x2/16dx=12∫11+(x/4)2dx

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent ∫11+u2du=arctan⁡u+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (x4)2.

So, let's substitute u=x4. Differentiating, we get dudx=14⟹dx=4du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫816+x2dx=12∫11+(x/4)2dx=12∫11+u2⋅(4du)=2∫du1+u2=2arctan⁡u+C=2arctan⁡(x4)+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{16+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8}{16\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/16)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/16}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{16+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =2\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =2\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=√8 x. Then dx=du/√8 and |x|=|u|/√8, so the integral becomes 8∫du/(|u|√(u²−1))=8 arcsec(√8 x)+C.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{8}{|x|\sqrt{8{x}^{2}-1}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{8\sqrt{8}}{|\sqrt{8}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{8}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{8}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{8}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{8}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{|x|\sqrt{8{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8\sqrt{8}}{|\sqrt{8}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{8}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\sqrt{8}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\text{d}u) \\  & =8\sqrt{8}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =8\,\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =8\,\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{8}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Calculate ∫8|x|8x2−1dx.

a
88arcsec(x)+C
b
arcsec(8x)+C
c
8arcsec(x8)+C
d
88arcsec(x)+C
e
8arcsec(8x)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that we can rewrite this integral as ∫8|x|8x2−1dx=∫88|8x|(8x)2−1dx.

This integral now resembles the basic one for arcsec, ∫1|u|u2−1du=arcsec(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u as the variable, we have 8x.

So, let's substitute u=8x. Differentiating, we get dudx=8⟹dx=18du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫8|x|8x2−1dx=∫88|8x|(8x)2−1dx=88∫1|u|u2−1⋅(18du)=88⋅18∫du|u|u2−1=8arcsec u+C=8arcsec(8x)+C

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant
content.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{8}{|x|\sqrt{8{x}^{2}-1}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{8\sqrt{8}}{|\sqrt{8}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{8}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{8}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{8}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{8}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{|x|\sqrt{8{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8\sqrt{8}}{|\sqrt{8}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{8}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\sqrt{8}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\text{d}u) \\  & =8\sqrt{8}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =8\,\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =8\,\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{8}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{8\,\text{d}x}{|8x|\sqrt{(8x)^{2}-1}}=8\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|8x|\sqrt{(8x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $8x.$

So, let's substitute $u=8x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=8\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}8\int \frac{1}{|8x|\sqrt{(8x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x & =8\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(8x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $3x.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(3x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant
content.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{7\,\text{d}x}{|7x|\sqrt{(7x)^{2}-1}}=7\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|7x|\sqrt{(7x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $7x.$

So, let's substitute $u=7x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=7\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{7}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}7\int \frac{1}{|7x|\sqrt{(7x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x & =7\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{7}\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(7x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=√3 x. Then dx=du/√3 and |x|=|u|/√3, so the factors cancel. The integral becomes ∫du/(|u|√(u²−1))=arcsec(√3 x)+C.

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{3{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{3}}{|\sqrt{3}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{3}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

$$

EXPLANATION

Note that we can rewrite this integral as ∫dx|x|3x2−1=∫3|3x|(3x)2−1dx.

This integral now resembles the basic one for arcsec, ∫1|u|u2−1du=arcsec(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u as the variable, we have 3x.

So, let's substitute u=3x. Differentiating, we get dudx=3⟹dx=13du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫1|x|3x2−1dx=∫3|3x|(3x)2−1dx=3∫1|u|u2−1⋅(13du)=3⋅13∫du|u|u2−1=arcsec u+C=arcsec(3x)+C

Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{3{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{3}}{|\sqrt{3}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{3}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{3{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{3}}{|\sqrt{3}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{3}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16

∫0331536−x2dx=
Submit

decision.explanation: An antiderivative is 15 arcsin(x/6). Evaluating at the bounds gives 15[arcsin(√3/2)−arcsin(0)]=15(π/3)=5π.

after.name: Question 16
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}\frac{15}{\sqrt{36-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =15{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{36\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/36)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/36}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/6)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{6}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=6\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $3\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}\frac{15}{\sqrt{36-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/6)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 6\,\text{d}u \\  & =15{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =15\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{3}/2} \\  & =15\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})-15\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =15\cdot \frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =5\pi \end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 17
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/3)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+(x/\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+(x/\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}/3}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}/3}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{3}/3} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{9}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since √(3−12x²)=√3√(1−4x²), an antiderivative is (√3/2)arcsin(2x). Evaluating gives (√3/2)[π/6−(−π/6)]=√3π/6.

after.name: Question 18
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-12{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3\cdot (1-4{x}^{2})}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

  

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(2x)}^{2}.$   

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-0.25$ | $0.25$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-0.5$ | $0.5$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-12{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.25}^{0.25}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.5}^{0.5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{\int }_{-0.5}^{0.5}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{-0.5}^{0.5} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0.5)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-0.5)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

∫−0.250.2533−12x2dx=3∫−0.250.2513⋅(1−4x2)dx=33∫−0.250.2511−4x2dx=3∫−0.250.2511−(2x)2dx

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine, ∫11−u2du=arcsin⁡(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u2 as the variable, we have (2x)2.

So, let's substitute u=2x. Differentiating, we get

dudx=2⟹dx=12du.

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from x to u.

x −0.25 0.25
u −0.5 0.5

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫−0.250.2533−12x2dx=3∫−0.250.2511−(2x)2dx=3∫−0.50.511−u2⋅(12du)=32∫−0.50.5du1−u2=32arcsin⁡u|−0.50.5=32(arcsin⁡(0.5)−arcsin⁡(−0.5))=32(π6+π6)=32⋅π3=3π6

decision.explanation: Factor the denominator as √5√(1−16x²) and substitute u=4x. The integral becomes (√5/2)∫₀^{1/2}du/√(1−u²)=(√5/2)arcsin(1/2)=√5π/12.

after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/8}\frac{10}{\sqrt{5-80{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =10{\int }_{0}^{1/8}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5(1-16{x}^{2})}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}}{\int }_{0}^{1/8}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-16{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{1/8}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(4x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine, 

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(4x)}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u.
